topic: Define: customer voice, CTQs, charter and scope

notes.front: What is the voice of the customer (VOC)?
notes.back: The customer's stated and unstated needs or requirements.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio lists many ways to capture it, among them interviews, surveys, focus groups, observation and complaint logs.
notes.example: Like a restaurant reading its reviews and watching what diners leave on their plates, but for any process.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “VOC – Voice of the Customer”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the Kano model?
notes.back: A tool for classifying and prioritising customer needs.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio says customer needs are not all of one kind or importance, and differ between populations, so the results help a team prioritise its effort.
notes.example: Like sorting a car's features into ones buyers take for granted and ones that pleasantly surprise them.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Kano model”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a critical to quality (CTQ) characteristic?
notes.back: A feature of a design, or of a part, that the customer regards as essential to its quality.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio treats CTQs as internal quality parameters, set apart from the customer's own critical requirements, to which they relate.
notes.example: Like the seal and panel fit a carmaker specifies so that a door shuts with the solid sound buyers expect.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Critical To Quality (CTQ)”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a CTQ tree?
notes.back: A tree diagram that turns a general customer need into specific, measurable critical to quality characteristics.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam calls this translation of vague wants into measurable specifications one of the objectives of the Define phase.
notes.example: Like breaking “a comfortable flat” down into room temperature, noise level and floor area, each with a number.
notes.source: MoreSteam, EngineRoom help, “CTQC Diagram”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a project charter?
notes.back: A document that sets out a Six Sigma project's mission and scope, and authorises the team to use organisational resources on it.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam says it gives the team high-level direction by answering basic questions, such as the goal, why it matters and how success will be measured.
notes.example: Like a signed brief for a building job, stating what will be built, why, by whom and by when.
notes.source: MoreSteam, EngineRoom help, “Project Charter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a problem statement in a DMAIC project?
notes.back: The statement, written in the Define phase, of the problem the project will tackle, together with its improvement goals.
notes.explanation: In MoreSteam's project charter, the problem statement answers the question of why the team is pursuing its goal.
notes.example: Like a patient's description of symptoms at the start of an appointment, before any tests are ordered.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 3, “Method and Implementation Approach”; MoreSteam, EngineRoom help, “Project Charter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a SMART goal?
notes.back: A goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio expands the acronym into these five words; each can be used as a check on a draft goal.
notes.example: Like “run 5 km in under 30 minutes by June” rather than “get fitter”.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “SMART”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the includes/excludes tool?
notes.back: A tool that helps a team set its project's boundaries by agreeing what is included in, and excluded from, the scope.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio adds that it opens discussion of scope issues and challenges the team to reach agreement.
notes.example: Like agreeing before a kitchen refit that the cupboards are in but the plumbing is out.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Includes/Excludes”, p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a SIPOC?
notes.back: A process map that sorts the elements of a process into five categories: Supplier, Input, Process, Output and Customer.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam says building one helps clarify a project's scope, by capturing the full breadth of related activities, which is often wider than it first seems.
notes.example: Like a recipe card that also lists the shops, the ingredients, the dish and the guests.
notes.source: MoreSteam, EngineRoom help, “SIPOC Map”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two of the questions the Starter Kit suggests asking about customers as part of the voice of the customer?
notes.back: For example: what do they want, and when do they want it?
notes.explanation: The kit says the answers help identify the value-added steps in a process and give design criteria for the final product.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit (version 4.0), “The ‘Voice of the Customer’ Data Considerations”, PDF p. 121 (printed p. 115)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team gathers complaint logs, warranty data and field reports to learn what customers need, whether or not they have said it outright. What is it capturing?
notes.choices:
A) The voice of the customer
B) The voice of the process
C) Critical to quality characteristics
D) The outputs in a SIPOC
notes.back: A: The voice of the customer.
notes.explanation: Complaint logs, warranty data and field reports are among LeanOhio's ways of capturing the customer's stated and unstated needs.
notes.choicesExplained: B: The voice of the process is what the process itself shows, such as whether it is in control. C: CTQs are internal quality characteristics that relate to customer needs. D: SIPOC outputs are what the process produces, not what customers need.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “VOC – Voice of the Customer”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: LeanOhio's four Kano need types are {{c1::Surprise or Delight}}, More is Better, Must Be things and Dis-satisfiers.
notes.explanation: Kano described these as types of customer need, or reactions to a product's characteristics and attributes.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Kano model”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: LeanOhio's four Kano need types are Surprise or Delight, {{c1::More is Better}}, Must Be things and Dis-satisfiers.
notes.explanation: The types exist because customer needs are not all of the same kind or the same importance.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Kano model”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: LeanOhio's four Kano need types are Surprise or Delight, More is Better, {{c1::Must Be}} things and Dis-satisfiers.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio credits the model to Kano, a Japanese researcher, who named these four types of customer need.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Kano model”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: LeanOhio's four Kano need types are Surprise or Delight, More is Better, Must Be things and {{c1::Dis-satisfiers}}.
notes.explanation: Sorting needs into these types lets a team prioritise its effort for different customers.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Kano model”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A bank has a long list of customer needs for its app and knows they differ in kind and importance between customer groups. Which tool helps it classify and prioritise them?
notes.choices:
A) SIPOC
B) Includes/excludes
C) Kano model
D) Force field analysis
notes.back: C: Kano model.
notes.explanation: Kano analysis classifies and prioritises customer needs, which differ in kind, in importance and between populations.
notes.choicesExplained: A: A SIPOC maps suppliers, inputs, process, outputs and customers; it does not rank needs. B: Includes/excludes sets the project's scope. D: Force field analysis maps driving and restraining forces on a solution.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Kano model”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does a critical-to-customer requirement differ from a CTQ, in LeanOhio's terms?
notes.back: The critical-to-customer item is the customer's own requirement; CTQs are the internal quality parameters that relate to it.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio says the two are not the same: the customer requirement feeds quality function deployment, which links it to the internal CTQs.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Critical to Customer”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Café customers say they want “hot coffee”. The team sets a serving temperature range for every cup. Which of these is a CTQ?
notes.choices:
A) The serving temperature range
B) The café's rating on a review site
C) The number of customer complaints
D) The customers' wish for hot coffee
notes.back: A: The serving temperature range.
notes.explanation: A CTQ is a characteristic of the product that is essential to quality in the customer's eyes; the temperature range is set internally to meet the customer's wish.
notes.choicesExplained: D: This is the customer's own requirement, which LeanOhio says is not the same as a CTQ. B: A review rating is not a characteristic of the coffee. C: Complaint logs are a way of capturing the voice of the customer.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Critical to Customer” and “Critical To Quality (CTQ)”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When building a CTQ tree, what question do you ask of each driver to find its CTQs?
notes.back: “What does that mean?”
notes.explanation: The tree runs from the need or problem statement on the left, through the drivers, to specific CTQs on the right.
notes.source: MoreSteam, EngineRoom help, “CTQC Diagram”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which tool can feed a CTQ tree, and where can its CTQs go next, according to MoreSteam?
notes.back: An affinity diagram's categories can become its drivers; its CTQs can then feed a cause-and-effect matrix or quality function deployment.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam places the CTQ tree between organising customer needs and setting specifications for the inputs that affect the CTQs.
notes.source: MoreSteam, EngineRoom help, “CTQC Diagram”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Patients say a clinic should be “easy to book”. The team splits this into drivers, then into measurable items such as days until the next free appointment. Which tool is it building?
notes.choices:
A) SIPOC
B) Force field analysis
C) CTQ tree
D) RACI matrix
notes.back: C: CTQ tree.
notes.explanation: A CTQ tree moves from a general need through drivers to specific, measurable characteristics.
notes.choicesExplained: A: A SIPOC sorts process elements from supplier to customer. B: Force field analysis lists driving and restraining forces. D: A RACI matrix sets out who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed.
notes.source: MoreSteam, EngineRoom help, “CTQC Diagram”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who approves a Six Sigma project charter, and its later revisions?
notes.back: The project Champion or sponsor approves it; as a controlled document, each revision is approved by the Champion and tracked.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam expects the charter to be refined and expanded continually as the team forms and takes action.
notes.source: MoreSteam, EngineRoom help, “Project Charter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two of the basic questions MoreSteam says a project charter answers?
notes.back: For example: what is the project's goal, and how will we measure success?
notes.explanation: Others include why the goal matters, how it relates to the business plan, who the players and stakeholders are, and when the project starts and ends.
notes.source: MoreSteam, EngineRoom help, “Project Charter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Black Belt wants to start spending staff time and budget on a new improvement project. Which document, once approved, gives the team that authority?
notes.choices:
A) Project charter
B) SIPOC
C) CTQ tree
D) Gantt chart
notes.back: A: Project charter.
notes.explanation: The approved charter authorises the team to dedicate organisational resources to the project.
notes.choicesExplained: B: A SIPOC maps the process and clarifies scope. C: A CTQ tree turns customer needs into measurable characteristics. D: A Gantt chart shows the schedule; it grants no authority.
notes.source: MoreSteam, EngineRoom help, “Project Charter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which three project roles does the Starter Kit's lean team charter name in its project details?
notes.back: Project sponsor(s), team leader(s) and facilitator(s).
notes.explanation: These roles lead the planning and running of the project; the kit's role descriptions also cover team members and the implementation team leader.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit (version 4.0), “Lean Team Charter”, PDF p. 114 (printed p. 108)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the lean team charter, what does the Project Scope section ask for?
notes.back: The start and end points of the process that the project will address.
notes.explanation: The template has two fields for this, Process Start and Process End, so the team fixes both ends of the process.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit (version 4.0), “Lean Team Charter”, PDF p. 114 (printed p. 108)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What goes in the lean team charter's Boundary Conditions section?
notes.back: The limits of the scope: what is excluded from the process, and which kinds of change are off limits to the team.
notes.explanation: It sits just after Project Scope, which fixes where the process starts and ends.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit (version 4.0), “Lean Team Charter”, PDF p. 114 (printed p. 108)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the lean team charter, what do the goals define?
notes.back: The desired outcomes of the project: what success looks like.
notes.explanation: Objectives then turn the goals into specific, measurable targets for improvement.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit (version 4.0), “Lean Team Charter”, PDF pp. 114–115 (printed pp. 108–109)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the lean team charter say objectives should be expressed if there is no current baseline data for the process?
notes.back: As percentage reductions.
notes.explanation: The template's metrics table shows the idea: a processing-time target of a 30% cut, with today's figure still to be measured at the event.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit (version 4.0), “Objectives and Performance Metrics”, PDF p. 115 (printed p. 109)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What follow-up schedule does the lean team charter template set out?
notes.back: Management meetings at 30, 60 and 90 days, plus any other key milestones.
notes.explanation: The template treats the dates as provisional: the team fixes them during the project, according to what it will need later.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit (version 4.0), “Follow-Up Schedule”, PDF p. 115 (printed p. 109)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: While drafting its lean team charter, a team writes: “No changes to the governing law or to the case-management software.” Which section does this belong in?
notes.choices:
A) Project Scope
B) Boundary Conditions
C) Goals
D) Follow-Up Schedule
notes.back: B: Boundary Conditions.
notes.explanation: Boundary Conditions records the limits of the scope, including which types of change are off limits to the team.
notes.choicesExplained: A: Project Scope gives the start and end points of the process. C: Goals describe what success looks like. D: The Follow-Up Schedule lists the 30-, 60- and 90-day meetings.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit (version 4.0), “Lean Team Charter”, PDF p. 114 (printed p. 108)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two things MoreSteam says a team should establish about a problem in the Define phase?
notes.back: For example: how big the problem is, and how often it occurs.
notes.explanation: The others are whom it affects and the conditions in which it arises.
notes.source: MoreSteam, What is the DMAIC Methodology? (blog), Define phase
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a SMART goal, what does the S stand for?
notes.back: Specific.
notes.explanation: “Reduce invoice errors” passes this test better than “improve finance”, because it names what is to change.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “SMART”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a SMART goal, what does the M stand for?
notes.back: Measurable.
notes.explanation: A goal such as “cut permit lead time from 90 to 45 days” can be checked with numbers; “speed up permits” cannot.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “SMART”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a SMART goal, what does the A stand for?
notes.back: Achievable.
notes.explanation: A target of zero errors by next week, for a process that has never come close, would fail this test.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “SMART”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a SMART goal, what does the R stand for?
notes.back: Relevant.
notes.explanation: A goal about repainting the office would fail this test on a project meant to cut billing errors.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “SMART”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a SMART goal, what does the T stand for?
notes.back: Time-bound.
notes.explanation: Adding “by 31 March” to a target turns an open-ended wish into a goal with a deadline.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “SMART”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A draft project goal reads: “Cut invoice errors from 8% to 2%.” Which SMART element does it plainly lack?
notes.choices:
A) Specific
B) Measurable
C) Achievable
D) Time-bound
notes.back: D: Time-bound.
notes.explanation: The goal names what is to change and gives start and target figures, but sets no date by which to reach them.
notes.choicesExplained: A: It names the thing to change, invoice errors. B: It gives a starting and a target figure. C: Nothing in the wording shows the target cannot be reached; the missing date is the clear gap.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “SMART”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does LeanOhio want a project's scope stated in specific detail?
notes.back: The more specific the in-scope and out-of-scope details, the less the project is likely to suffer scope creep.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio defines project scope as defined, specific beginning and end points for the project.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Project Scope”, p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Midway through a project on invoice approval, a manager asks the team to fix supplier registration too. Which tool, used at the start, gives the team an agreed basis for answering?
notes.choices:
A) Affinity diagram
B) Kano model
C) Program evaluation and review technique
D) Includes/excludes
notes.back: D: Includes/excludes.
notes.explanation: Includes/excludes records what the team agreed is inside and outside its scope, and is meant to prompt discussion of scope issues.
notes.choicesExplained: B: The Kano model classifies customer needs. C: PERT analyses a project's tasks and timings. A: An affinity diagram groups ideas by common thread.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Includes/Excludes”, p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a SIPOC, who provides a process's inputs?
notes.back: Suppliers.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio's summary of the chain starts here: inputs are obtained from suppliers.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “SIPOC”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a SIPOC, what does the process receive from its suppliers?
notes.back: Inputs.
notes.explanation: They are what the process then adds value to, before handing on an output.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “SIPOC”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a SIPOC, which element adds value to the inputs?
notes.back: The process.
notes.explanation: It sits in the middle of the chain, between the inputs from suppliers and the output to customers.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “SIPOC”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a SIPOC, which element should meet or exceed the customer's requirements?
notes.back: The output.
notes.explanation: The output is what the process provides once it has added value to the inputs.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “SIPOC”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a SIPOC, whose requirements set the standard the output must meet or exceed?
notes.back: The customers'.
notes.explanation: The chain ends with them: the output is judged against what the customer requires.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “SIPOC”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where does MoreSteam say you should start when building a SIPOC map?
notes.back: With the process steps; then work left to the inputs and their suppliers, and right to the outputs and their customers.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam calls starting from the processing steps and working backwards the best way to create one.
notes.source: MoreSteam, EngineRoom help, “SIPOC Map”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team begins its SIPOC by listing every possible supplier and stalls, unsure which ones matter. What does MoreSteam advise instead?
notes.choices:
A) Start from the process steps and work outwards
B) Replace the SIPOC with a Gantt chart
C) Start from the outputs alone
D) List all the customers first
notes.back: A: Start from the process steps and work outwards.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam says to start with the process steps, then identify inputs and suppliers to the left and outputs and customers to the right.
notes.choicesExplained: D: Starting from customers is not MoreSteam's advice; the process steps come first. B: A Gantt chart shows a schedule and does not map the process. C: Outputs are found by working right from the steps, not used as the starting point.
notes.source: MoreSteam, EngineRoom help, “SIPOC Map”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
